---
title: "The documents"
---

Before any of the stages make sense, it helps to have the cast in one place. A trial produces a
chain of documents and datasets, each written by different people, for different readers, at
different times. Most of the difficulty in what follows comes from the joins between them.

If you already work in one part of this chain, the useful thing here is probably the part you
don't touch.

## What a trial produces

| | What it is | Who writes it | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Protocol** | The plan of the trial in prose: why, who, what happens to them, what is measured, what will be concluded | Clinical, medical, with statistical input | What the trial *is* |
| **SAP** | Statistical analysis plan. How the data will be analysed — populations, models, handling of missing data, the exact tables | Statistics | What "analysed" means |
| **CRF** | Case report form. The screens or pages a site fills in for each subject | Data management | What gets collected |
| **SDTM** | Study Data Tabulation Model. The collected data, standardised — one domain per kind of observation, close to what was recorded | Programming | What was observed |
| **ADaM** | Analysis Data Model. Datasets built *for* the analysis, with derived values like change from baseline already computed. The ones this book uses have one row per subject per parameter per visit | Programming | What is analysed |
| **TFL** | Tables, figures and listings — the output a reader of the study actually sees | Programming | What is reported |

The important thing about **SDTM and ADaM** being separate: SDTM is meant to faithfully record
what happened, and ADaM is meant to be analysis-ready. Change from baseline does not exist in
SDTM — someone has to decide which record *is* the baseline and subtract it. That decision is
made in a programming specification, written in prose, and it is exactly the kind of decision
this whole chain is trying to make explicit.

## Where the standards in this book sit

Three things are being applied on top of that chain, and they address different joins in it.

**ICH M11** is a template for the protocol itself. Fourteen sections, and in its electronic form
a list of data elements, each with a code — so a protocol stops being free prose and starts
being a structure that can be read by something other than a person. It addresses the protocol
alone.

**USDM** — the Unified Study Definition Model — is the protocol *as data*. Objectives,
endpoints, estimands, arms, populations, the schedule of activities, expressed as JSON against a
defined model. If M11 says what a protocol must contain, USDM is a shape that content can live
in and be queried from.

**AC/DC** — Analysis and Derivation Concepts — covers the other end: how a measurement becomes
an analysis result. Three kinds of thing:

- an **observation concept**, the atomic measured thing
- a **derivation concept**, a step that computes — select a baseline, subtract it, window a visit
- an **analysis concept**, the aggregated result — a comparison, a model, a summary

A **biomedical concept** sits underneath, as the standard definition of the thing being
measured: serum alanine aminotransferase, with its units, codes and permissible values.

Between them they cover the two ends and the join: M11 structures the sentence, USDM makes it
addressable, AC/DC declares what happens to the measurement. That is the path described in the
introduction — every step declared rather than implied — laid against the documents a trial
actually produces.

## The join this book is about

The study definition drives two things, not one. It says what will be *measured* — which becomes
a case report form, and through it the collected data — and it says what will be *concluded*,
which becomes the analysis. The two meet again at the end.

```
            protocol ──M11──▶ structured protocol ──USDM──▶ study as data
                                                                  │
              ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
              │ schedule of activities:                objectives, endpoints,    │
              │ what is measured, and when             estimands: what is asked  │
              ▼                                                                  │
             CRF ──collection──▶ SDTM ──derivation──▶ ADaM                        │
                                                       │                         │
                                                       └──── AC/DC ◀─────────────┘
                                                                │
                                                                ▼
                                                            a result
```

The **CRF** sits on the left-hand branch: the schedule of activities says a subject has
chemistry taken at a given visit, and the case report form is where that becomes a field
somebody fills in. In the study definition, that link is made by an activity naming the concepts
it collects:

{{json:study/usdm/toriva-lung-301.usdm.json#study.versions[0].studyDesigns[0].activities[5].biomedicalConceptIds}}

That is the *Chemistry (LFTs, creatinine)* activity, naming five biomedical concepts. In this
study the link is present on the activities the two chains end in and not on the rest of the
schedule — it is made deliberately, one terminal at a time, and
[stage 2](stage-2-bc.qmd) is where.

This is where the biomedical concept earns its keep, and why it is worth understanding early:
**the same definition is supposed to govern both branches.** The concept that says what serum
alanine aminotransferase is — its units, its code, its permissible values — should determine the
field on the form, the variable in the collected data, and the thing the derivation binds to at
the far end. One definition, used at both ends, rather than a chain of people agreeing to mean
the same thing.

**This book walks the right-hand branch only.** It starts from analysis datasets that already
exist, and takes them to a result. The collection side — CRF design, and the path from a
completed form to standardised data — is a substantial subject in its own right and is not
exercised here. It is drawn because leaving it out makes the study definition look like an input
to analysis alone, which is the smaller half of what it is for.

## Where the concepts come from

Nothing in the stages that follow is invented at the keyboard. Every stage is a choice from a
published list, and it helps to know the lists before meeting them.

**Biomedical concepts come from the CDISC Library**, where each is published once, with its
code and its properties. A study does not define them. Its definition carries a copy of the ones
its schedule of activities collects, and each copy keeps the address it was taken from:

{{json:study/usdm/toriva-lung-301.usdm.json#study.versions[0].biomedicalConcepts[0].reference}}

**Derivation and analysis concepts come from CDISC's analysis-concepts repository**, which
publishes three different kinds of thing. The stages use all three, and telling them apart is
most of what makes the choices readable:

| | What it is | Example | Where it is published |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Concept** | A kind of value. A derivation concept is a value computed for each subject; an analysis concept is a result computed across subjects | `Change`; `Contrasts` | The concept models, `model/concept/` |
| **Method** | A computation and the roles it needs filled. It knows nothing about any study | `M.Subtraction` needs a minuend and a subtrahend; `M.ANCOVA` a response, a covariate and a fixed effect | The method library, `lib/methods/` |
| **Template** | A method with its roles already bound to concepts. The library's own word is *transformation* | `T.ChangeFromBaseline`: `M.Subtraction`, producing a `Change` from two measurements | The transformation library, `lib/transformations/` |

**What you select is almost always a template.** The concept says what you want, the template
is how the library offers it, and the method is what the template runs. Stages 3 and 4 show one
of each, as published.

So when a stage says *choose*, there is a list being chosen from and a sentence in one of the
study's documents that decides it:

| You choose | From | Decided by |
|---|---|---|
| Biomedical concepts — stage 2 | The concepts the study definition carries, copied from the CDISC Library | The protocol's schedule: what is collected |
| A derivation template — stage 3 | The transformation library's derivation templates | The analysis plan's derivation rule: how the analysed value is computed |
| An analysis template — stage 4 | The transformation library's analysis templates | The analysis plan's model |
| The slice — parameter, visit, population, treatments — stage 4 | The study definition | The estimand, or the plan's analysis |

**The stages are in the order of the concepts, which is not the order a tool asks in.** What is
measured, how it is derived, how it is analysed is the order that explains the model. Authoring
runs the other way, because each choice decides what the next one has to supply: the analysis
says what must be derived, and the derivation says which measurements it needs. The table under
[The application used here](#the-application-used-here) shows which of its steps does which
stage's work.

## The worked example

One analysis is carried through every stage: **change from baseline in alanine aminotransferase
at Cycle 2 Day 1, in the safety population, compared between the two arms by ANCOVA with the
baseline value as covariate.**

Each part of that sentence has a source, and they are not all the same one:

- **The endpoint is the protocol's.** Laboratory evaluations are a safety endpoint, and the
  study definition's text for it says they are "analysed as change from baseline".
- **The baseline rule is the analysis plan's**: the last value on or before the first dose.
- **The parameter, the visit and the model are this book's choice.** They were chosen to exercise the
  chain, not taken from the study's plan, and the restructured protocol records them as a
  demonstration analysis. A real study would take all three from its plan.

The stages that follow walk the right-hand branch on that analysis, stage by stage, and stop
where it produces a number — then compare that number against the same model fitted on the
datasets a programmer built from the same plan. A second analysis, systolic blood pressure under
a repeated-measures model, is the same kind of choice. It joins at stages 6 and 7, where its
result and its divergence are shown beside the first.

## The application used here

The chapters keep saying *in the application used here*. This is what that application is.

**It is CDISC's own, and it lives beside the concepts.** The analysis-concepts repository that
publishes the concept models and the libraries also carries a browser application, in its
`ac-dc-app/` directory, which it calls the **eSAP Builder** and describes as demonstrating the
framework end to end. This book did not write it. It is a demonstration of the framework rather
than a product, which is why the chapters treat what it does as true of one tool at one commit.

**Everything it offers comes from the published files.** At start-up it reads the study
definition, the concept models, the transformation library, the method library and the method
implementations, and builds its lists from them. So when a step offers nine templates, those
are nine entries in the library, not a choice the application made.

**It has eight steps, and they do not line up one-to-one with the stages:**

| Step | What it does | Stage in this book |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Select Study | Lists the study definitions it has been given | 1 |
| 2. Study Overview | Shows the study: arms, objectives and endpoints, schedule | 1 |
| 3. Endpoint | The concept the endpoint is about, and the slice | 3 and 4 |
| 4. Analysis | The analysis template | 4 |
| 5. Summary | A review of what has been set | — |
| 6. Derivations | The chain as a graph: where each input comes from, and the biomedical concepts | 2 and 3 |
| 7. eSAP Builder | The generated plan | 5 |
| 8. Execute | Runs the chain against datasets | 6 |

**Two words are used for its two halves.** The *builder* is steps 1 to 7, where a chain is
authored and saved. The *engine* is what step 8 runs: R code, executed in the browser under
WebR, which reads the saved specification and the datasets and returns the result.

**How it is run here.** The setup chapter serves it from the pinned copy of CDISC's repository,
with this book's material placed into it: the study definition, the study's datasets in the
format the engine reads, the saved chains, and the one method implementation the colophon
names. Stopping the server takes them out again.

## A note on versions

All three standards are moving, and so is the tooling. This book describes:

- **ICH M11** in its merged electronic form, as mapped in the factory's `study/m11/`
- **USDM v4.0**
- CDISC's **analysis-concepts** repository at the commit this repository pins, which every
  screenshot here is stamped with

That is deliberate. A guide that claims to be current is wrong within a release; one that says
which version it describes stays useful, because you can tell what has moved since.
